I hear the phrase being used a lot, but I rarely get any context for it.

The idea that all cultural are of equal importance/value. People hate it because

  • It places uncivilized cultures on the same level as civilized culture
  • It's used to downplay attacks performed by a member of said uncivilized culture (eg, guy kills some people, everyone says its racism and not everyone does that yadayadayada)
  • It's also used as a reason to prevent people from enjoying their own culture (because that means you don't like everyone else as much)

The subject also tends expands to religion and nationalism - because under cultural marxism all religions are the same and all countries are the same.

• It places uncivilized cultures on the same level as civilized culture

Rather, it argues that it is impossible to define "civilized" in a meaningful fashion, so the label of "uncivilized" is simply a subjective condemnation of cultures which hold values that your own culture has rejected. In some circumstances, this argument makes a level of sense: consider two cultures, one of which considers capital punishment to be a barbaric expression of bloodlust (but lifetime imprisonment humane) and another which considers lifetime imprisonment to be a barbaric form of torture (but capital punishment a more humane alternative). From an outside perspective neither of those understandings are necessarily insane, but both cultures will nonetheless label the other as barbaric and uncivilized.

On the other hand, there are certain moral concepts which are unambiguously more adaptive than their alternatives, and other moral concepts (or laws, or rules) which have rapidly become global norms. (Moreover, the two sometimes conflict.) Because of this many argue that it is in fact possible to outline at least some objective and universal (or at least global) forms of morality, which doesn't play nicely with purely relativistic views. After that, we're into philosophy and it gets genuinely complicated (but somewhat less bullshit).

TL;DR: It's not that it places "uncivilized" cultures on the same level as "civilized" ones, it's that it claims all definitions of "civilized" are arbitrary and self-serving. Perhaps that's an academic distinction, but I'd say it's an important one nonetheless.

Edit: (also, as pointed out by musa_acuminata below, you're actually talking about cultural relativism, not cultural marxism. It's a common mistake, mostly because cultural marxism almost always appears within a relativist framework, but they're really not the same thing. Serves me right for not paying attention to OP.)

It's most commonly encountered as a snarl word decrying everything right-wingers don't like, alluding to a conspiracy theory involving sinister left-wingers in the cultural and artistic spheres, including the media and academia, supposedly being engaged in a decades-long plot to undermine Western culture, with bonus anti-Semitism.

In legitimate academic circles, the term describes the post-Second World War influence of Marxist thought on cultural studies, notably through the work of the Frankfurt school. Although Marx never wrote at any length about culture (what he deemed "the superstructure"), cultural theorists have often used the lens of class, alongside other factors such as race, gender, and sexuality to understand how culture works to perpetuate social inequality. The term "cultural Marxism" was first sighted around 1973, in The Critique of Domination: The Origins and Development of Critical Theory by Trent Schroyer.

Outside of graduate seminars in intellectual history, the term is primarily used by reactionaries to red-bait anyone with progressive tendencies.
